Medical eligibility criteria for contraceptive use, 6th ed. 2025
novedades.texto: Etonogestrel subdermal implant (Implanon/Nexplanon, 1 rod): approved duration of 5 years — already approved by the US FDA (January 2026), UK MHRA (May 2026), ANMAT Argentina (2025 — also covering already-placed implants), and ANVISA Brazil (October 2026 — which also authorized immediate postpartum and post-abortion insertion, 1st and 2nd trimester). Based on trial MK-8415-060 (NCT04626596, Merck/Organon): 0 pregnancies in years 4 and 5, Pearl Index 0.0 (95% CI 0-0.69), no difference by BMI (the trial included BMI 17.2-64.3, 38.1% with BMI ≥30 — the updated label no longer warns of reduced efficacy at high BMI). It does not "run out" at 3 years: etonogestrel release declines slowly (label: ~60-70 mcg/day at weeks 5-6, ~35-45 mcg/day at the end of year 1, ~25-30 mcg/day at the end of year 3), and median serum levels stay above 90 pg/mL — the anovulation threshold — across all BMI categories through year 5 (McNicholas 2017). Independent extended-use studies agree: McNicholas 2015 (CHOICE: 123 users completed year 4 and 34 year 5, 0 pregnancies), McNicholas 2017 (291 users, 444 woman-years, 0 pregnancies; year-4 failure: 0 [97.5% CI 0-1.48], year-5: 0 [0-2.65]) and Ali et al. 2016 (390 women with extended use, 0 pregnancies in years 4 and 5). Dominant mechanism: suppression of ovulation (anovulation) + thickening of cervical mucus. Immediate reversibility upon removal. ⚠️ Paraguay: the current national MSPBS guideline (Manual Nacional de Normas de Planificación Familiar, 3rd ed. 2021) still states 3 years, with earlier replacement if BMI ≥30 — it has not incorporated this update. Until MSPBS updates its guideline, in Paraguay's public sector record the insertion date and explain both criteria to the patient (international regulatory agencies vs. the current national guideline). CaVeSal® own algorithm · Based on: FDA 2026, MHRA 2026, ANMAT 2025, ANVISA 2026, McNicholas 2015 and 2017, Ali 2016, MSPBS 2021. 2-rod levonorgestrel implant (Jadelle/Norplant-2/Sino-Implant): 5 years. Mechanism somewhat different from etonogestrel: endometrial atrophy and the cervical mucus plug predominate over suppression of ovulation (which is more variable with this implant). LNG-IUS (levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system) — 3 distinct doses/durations, not a single one: LNG 52mg (Mirena/Liletta/Levosert/Asertia): 8 years. LNG 19.5mg (Kyleena): 5 years. LNG 13.5mg (Jaydess/Skyla — sometimes marketed as a hormonal "Mini IUD", not to be confused with the copper mini-IUD in the following row): 3 years, with lower serum LNG levels and greater preservation of ovulatory cycles than the higher doses. Copper IUD — duration depends on copper load/frame size, not a single value: High-load (TCu380A and equivalents, e.g. Multiload 375, Nova T, Flexi, T Cu 380A): 10-12 years per WHO (the range depends on the specific product). Reduced-frame/"mini" copper IUD (smaller copper surface area, usually reserved for nulliparous patients or small uterine cavities): shorter duration, typically on the order of 5 years — confirm against the specific model/brand's insert, since a lower copper load corresponds to a shorter approved duration. Silver-core IUD (Cu-Ag, e.g. Andalan Silverflex): the silver core slows fragmentation/oxidation of the copper wire inside the uterus — a mechanism that in theory extends the device's useful life relative to a pure copper IUD. However, at least one regional manufacturer labels its "Silver T" presentation with a duration of 5 years, shorter than that of high-load copper IUDs — ⚠️ there is real variability between brands/markets; confirm the duration against the specific brand's insert used in your practice before treating it as a single figure for this guide. Regarding silver's "bactericidal" effect: ionic silver does have well-documented general antibacterial activity in the microbiology/materials literature — but the source educational material (AC Hormonal 2025) specifically describes silver's role in the IUD as slowing copper fragmentation, not as a local anti-infective mechanism aimed at reducing PID; ⚠️ I did not find a gynecology-specific source documenting a clinically relevant bactericidal effect of the silver core on pelvic infection risk — if you have a specific reference for that, happy to add it. All IUDs/IUSs are also useful as post-coital emergency contraception (see following guide). Non-contraceptive benefits of the LNG-IUS: significantly reduces menstrual bleeding (therapeutic use in AUB, see corresponding guide), and offers some relative protection against symptomatic PID compared with the copper IUD. Contraindications (MEC Cat 4): see the WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria guide — distortion of the uterine cavity, active pelvic infection, untreated cervical/endometrial cancer (IUDs in general); active breast cancer (LNG-IUS, due to the hormonal component).

novedades.titulo: MHT and cardiovascular risk — Joint FIGO/WHF position
novedades.fuentes: Benedetto C, Gulati M, Khadilkar SS, et al., on behalf of the World Heart Federation (WHF) and the International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO). Menopause hormone therapy in women with cardiovascular risk factors or established ischemic heart disease: A joint FIGO and WHF position paper. Int J Gynecol Obstet. 2026. DOI: 10.1002/ijgo.71356
novedades.texto: Window of opportunity: systemic MHT started within 10 years of the FMP or before age 60 keeps the most favorable cardiovascular risk-benefit profile (↓ all-cause mortality, ↓ composite outcome of CV death and non-fatal MI in RCT meta-analyses). Starting it beyond that window should not be considered for a cardioprotective purpose — see also MRS scale and Hormone Replacement Therapy. CV risk stratification before prescribing MHT (symptomatic woman, within 10 years of the FMP): assess family and personal CVD history. Low risk: no restrictions on MHT type, dose or route. High risk: low-dose transdermal estrogen, combined with micronized progesterone or dydrogesterone if the uterus is intact. Intermediate risk (e.g., an estimated 10-year CV event risk of 5-7% on standard calculators such as SCORE2): when feasible, coronary artery calcium score by CT (CAC-CT) — CAC = 0 suggests very low CV risk; CAC ≤10 reclassifies the patient as low risk (no MHT restrictions); CAC >10 confirms high-risk management (transdermal + a safer progestogen). In any category, treat hypertension and other modifiable risk factors before or alongside starting MHT. Established ischemic heart disease: differentiate the subtype before deciding on management. INOCA (ischemia with nonobstructive CAD) and MINOCA (myocardial infarction with nonobstructive CAD): if MHT had already been started within 10 years of the FMP, discontinuing it may be unnecessary. Obstructive coronary disease and SCAD (spontaneous coronary artery dissection): insufficient evidence on MHT use — individualized management, with particular caution in SCAD. Across all 4 categories, if MHT is continued or started: low-dose transdermal estrogen + micronized progesterone or dydrogesterone (intact uterus), concurrent primary and secondary prevention (statins, antihypertensives, antiplatelet therapy as appropriate) and multidisciplinary management (cardiology + gynecology). Progestogen and differentiated thrombotic/cerebrovascular risk: micronized progesterone and dydrogesterone — no significant increase in VTE risk, oral or transdermal (the safer option). ⚠️ Higher VTE risk: oral estrogen of any type, and transdermal estradiol combined with norpregnane/pregnane or nortestosterone derivatives (e.g., medroxyprogesterone acetate, nomegestrol acetate) — the risk increases from the start of treatment. Norethisterone acetate (NETA): uncertain risk, insufficient evidence. ⚠️ Tibolone: not associated with higher VTE risk, but is associated with higher ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke risk — consider especially with a history of stroke or high cerebrovascular risk. Route and dose across scenarios: in any high CV risk scenario, intermediate risk reclassified as high, or established ischemic heart disease, the preferred combination is low-dose transdermal estrogen + micronized progesterone or dydrogesterone (if uterus intact) — consistent with the route/dose already recommended in MRS scale and Hormone Replacement Therapy for hypertension, obesity and VTE risk. Key messages (FIGO/WHF summary): menopause is a critical window for cardiovascular assessment and prevention. Early MHT initiation relieves climacteric symptoms and may be associated with reduced all-cause mortality and reduced composite cardiovascular outcome. Risk stratification is mandatory before prescribing: type, dose and route must be individualized. In high risk, the transdermal + micronized progesterone/dydrogesterone combination is the preferred option. In established ischemic heart disease, MHT may be considered for symptomatic relief after counseling and shared decision-making. Always maintain concurrent primary and secondary prevention (statins, blood pressure control) and use multidisciplinary management for complex cases.

novedades.titulo: MRS scale and Hormone Replacement Therapy
novedades.fuentes: NAMS Position Statement (2022) · Heinemann et al. (2004) · Manual para Manejo de la Mujer en Edad del Climaterio, 2nd ed. (SOCHEG, 2020) · Stute P, et al. EMAS 2026 framework, Maturitas 2026;212:109060 · MSPyBS Paraguay Res. S.G. No. 267/2023 · ACOG Clinical Practice Guideline No. 13. Management of Menopause-Related Vasomotor, Sleep, and Mood Symptoms. Obstet Gynecol. 2026;148(5):e345-e364
novedades.texto: MRS (11 items): somatic, psychological, urogenital. NAMS/Heinemann scheme (total score only): 0-4 mild · 5-8 moderate · ≥9 severe (consider HRT). SOCHEG scheme (broken down by domain, each with its own severe-alteration cutoff): Somatic (items 1-4) ≥8 · Psychological (items 5-8) ≥6 · Urogenital (items 9-11) ≥3 · Total (items 1-11) ≥15. HRT by uterine status: no uterus → estrogen alone. Uterus present, perimenopause → sequential/cyclic. Postmenopause → continuous combined. Transdermal HRT (preferred, especially with hypertension, obesity BMI>30, hypertriglyceridemia, VTE risk): 17β-Estradiol gel 0.75-1.25g/day, or patches 25-50mcg/day. Endometrial protection (intact uterus): Micronized natural progesterone 200mg/day for 10-14 days/month (sequential regimen) or 100mg/day continuous · or Dydrogesterone 10-20mg/day. Tibolone (STEAR): 2.5mg/day PO (or 1.25mg/day in lower body weight or advanced perimenopause) — covers vasomotor symptoms, urogenital atrophy and bone loss prevention (estrogen doses to prevent bone loss and what to do when MHT is stopped: see Osteoporosis and bone densitometry); does not require an added progestogen. Tissue-selective estrogen complex (alternative when avoiding a progestogen is preferred): Conjugated equine estrogens 0.45mg/day + Bazedoxifene 20mg/day — bazedoxifene (a SERM) replaces the progestogen for endometrial protection, without the bleeding or breast tenderness associated with it. Evidence from the SMART-1/SMART-2 trials (12 weeks): significant reduction in hot flush frequency/severity vs. placebo, with a 50% reduction by day 8-10 and a sustained ~90% reduction by day 83 of use; no increased risk of breast cancer, endometrial cancer, VTE, stroke or coronary disease in pooled analyses (follow-up up to 2 years — confidence limited by low event incidence and lack of longer-term data). ⚠️ Availability in Paraguay not confirmed — verify locally before prescribing. Alternative endometrial protection — 52mg LNG-IUD: off-label use alongside systemic estrogen to provide endometrial protection (plus contraception if applicable) — replace at 5 years when used for this purpose (the approved contraceptive lifespan is 8 years, but the evidence supporting endometrial protection in HRT covers up to 5 years). Local availability (Paraguay, confirm against the current pharmacy/distributor): transdermal 17β-estradiol gel/spray (e.g., Ginoderm) — available. 17β-estradiol vaginal ring — not available. Conjugated equine estrogens + bazedoxifene — availability unconfirmed. This information is contextual, to anticipate the availability conversation with the patient — it should not be used to exclude an option from the clinical list. Interaction with GLP-1/GIP agonists: the gastric emptying delay induced by semaglutide/tirzepatide (more pronounced with the latter) may reduce absorption of oral HRT — in patients on GLP-1/GIP therapy, prefer the transdermal route for estrogen therapy (same pharmacokinetic principle as in the Contraception during tirzepatide guide).

novedades.fuentes: NOF/BHOF (2022) · AACE/ACE (2020) · WHO Criteria · Stute P, et al. EMAS 2026 framework, Maturitas 2026;212:109060 · MSPyBS Paraguay Res. S.G. No. 267/2023 · McClung MR, Clark AL. Preventing menopause-related bone loss. Menopause 2026;33(11):1209-1211 · Bolland MJ, et al. NEJM 2025;392:239-248 · The Menopause Society (2021, 2022) · USPSTF (2022)
novedades.texto: T-Score: normal ≥-1.0 · osteopenia -1.0 to -2.5 · osteoporosis ≤-2.5 · severe +fracture. Z-Score (premenopausal): ≤-2.0 abnormal. FRAX (osteopenia, established postmenopause): treat if major fracture risk ≥20% or hip ≥3%. FRAX and OST are not useful to identify perimenopausal women who will develop osteoporosis. Basic support (all patients): Elemental calcium 1,000-1,500mg/day + Vitamin D3 800-2,000 IU/day (target ≥30ng/mL). Antiresorptives: Alendronate 70mg PO weekly · Risedronate 35mg weekly or 150mg monthly · Zoledronic acid 5mg IV annually · Denosumab 60mg SC every 6 months (do not stop abruptly without transitioning to another antiresorptive, due to rebound vertebral fracture risk). Anabolics (severe osteoporosis/high fracture risk): Teriparatide 20mcg/day SC, maximum 24 months of use. Prevention of bone loss in perimenopause and menopause Prevention ≠ treatment: treatment is given to women at high current fracture risk; prevention aims to maintain bone density so that osteoporosis does not develop later. Bone loss is fastest in the year before and the first years after the final menstrual period (≈10% at the spine and ≈9% at the hip at 5 years, almost 1 T-score unit); abrupt estrogen withdrawal (oophorectomy, stopping MHT) accelerates it. Higher risk: the best predictor is bone density on entering perimenopause — with a T-score <−1.0 most women reach osteoporosis (≤−2.5) before age 65. Risk factors for low BMD: weight <57 kg, prolonged amenorrhea after puberty or delayed puberty (Turner syndrome, exercise-related amenorrhea), previous fracture, family history of osteoporosis, illnesses or drugs that harm the skeleton. Densitometry (DXA): in every perimenopausal woman with any of these factors, to identify those with a T-score <−1.0 who benefit most from prevention. Nutrition, supplements and exercise: advisable for all women, but they do not prevent menopause-related bone loss (calcium, vitamin D, vitamin K2, collagen, phytoestrogens and the various exercise regimens at best slow it modestly). Estrogen: oral, transdermal or systemic-dose vaginal MHT prevents bone loss for as long as it is used (also combined with a progestogen or bazedoxifene) and reduces spine and hip fractures by 30–40%. Consider it in women reaching menopause with a T-score <−1.0. Best response in early postmenopause with oral estradiol 2mg or a 0.1mg/day patch; in perimenopause, contraceptives with 20µg ethinyl estradiol are effective. Lower doses protect a smaller proportion of women (the 0.014mg patch was only studied in late postmenopause, ages 60–80). No serum estradiol target has been validated; with transdermal products it can be measured to check absorption. No fixed duration limit; individualize. When estrogen is stopped: the bone benefit is lost within 12 months. Give a bisphosphonate for 2–3 years (alendronate, or one zoledronic acid infusion), then raloxifene or intermittent bisphosphonate to maintain density. If estrogen is contraindicated: approved for prevention are raloxifene (weak effect, does not fully prevent loss) and the bisphosphonates alendronate, ibandronate, risedronate and zoledronate. For prevention, alendronate and zoledronate are used at half the treatment dose: alendronate 35mg PO weekly for 3–5 years, or zoledronic acid 2 doses 2 years apart; then intermittent bisphosphonate. MHT without vasomotor symptoms: The Menopause Society considers it reasonable to prevent bone loss in women at high risk of osteoporosis; the USPSTF (2022) recommends against MHT for the primary prevention of chronic conditions. Use shared decision-making. CaVeSal® own algorithm · Based on: McClung MR, Clark AL. Menopause 2026;33(11):1209-1211 (The Menopause Society) · Bolland MJ, et al. NEJM 2025 · USPSTF 2022.

novedades.titulo: Vitamin K2 (MK-7) — Bone and vascular health
novedades.fuentes: Knapen MHJ, Drummen NE, Smit E, Vermeer C, Theuwissen E. Three-year low-dose menaquinone-7 supplementation helps decrease bone loss in healthy postmenopausal women. Osteoporos Int. 2013;24(9):2499-2507 · Vossen LM, de Leeuw PW, Schurgers LJ, et al. Two Years of Menaquinone-7 Supplementation and Coronary Artery Calcification: A Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA Cardiol. 2026 (online Jun 10, 2026). doi:10.1001/jamacardio.2026.1279
novedades.texto: Mechanism: vitamin K2 is a cofactor for the carboxylation of vitamin K-dependent proteins — it activates osteocalcin (calcium binding to bone) and matrix Gla protein/MGP (an inhibitor of soft-tissue calcification, including the arterial wall). Distinct from vitamin K1 (dietary, predominantly hepatic/coagulation-related). Bone (Knapen et al. 2013, RCT, n=244 healthy postmenopausal women, 3 years): MK-7 180mcg/day decreased age-related loss of bone mineral content (BMC) and bone mineral density (BMD) at the lumbar spine and femoral neck (not at total hip), improved femoral neck bone strength indices, and reduced loss of vertebral height in the lower thoracic region. The source consulted does not publish the exact percentage BMD change figures or p-values — refer to the original article for those numbers before citing them with decimal precision. Vascular (Vossen et al., VitaK-CAC, JAMA Cardiology 2026, RCT, n=167 with symptomatic coronary artery disease and coronary calcium 50-400 AU, 2 years): MK-7 360mcg/day modestly slowed progression of coronary calcification (Agatston score) vs. placebo (between-group difference p=0.02), with plasma MK-7 levels in the active arm rising from 0.50 to 6.56mcg/L (p<0.001). ⚠️ The authors and the accompanying editorial describe the effect as "modest" and of still-uncertain clinical significance — they call for larger, longer-follow-up trials before considering it an intervention with impact on hard cardiovascular events. No relevant adverse events were reported. Practical doses (per the evidence cited, two distinct contexts — not interchangeable): bone loss prevention in the climacteric: MK-7 180mcg/day (as an adjunct: supplements slow bone loss modestly but do not prevent menopause-related bone loss — see Prevention in the Osteoporosis guide). Cardiovascular context (established coronary disease): the dose studied was 360mcg/day, in a population with already-diagnosed heart disease — there is no equivalent evidence in general primary prevention. Combination with vitamin D3: both vitamins act on complementary axes of bone metabolism (D3 increases calcium absorption and osteocalcin synthesis; K2 activates/carboxylates it) — see the vitamin D3 dose in the Osteoporosis and bone densitometry guide (above).
